idiom_name: plain classes as states + self.state = NextState()
implementation_notes: Python needs neither an interface declaration nor a registry: a state is an ordinary object, the context stores it as an attribute and calls self.state.publish(self), and duck typing means only the operations actually called matter. Stateless states should be module-level singletons (or enum members) and carry no per-context data; abc.ABC with abstractmethod is worth adding only when several states must implement a rich interface and instantiation errors are wanted early. Delegation via __getattr__ can forward every unknown attribute to the current state, but it hides where a method really lives, so explicit forwarding methods are usually the better trade.
pitfalls: Only dynamic errors catch a missing method: a state without an operation fails at call time, so cover every (state, operation) pair with tests.
__getattr__-based delegation obscures tracebacks, help() and IDE navigation; prefer explicit methods or Forwardable-style listing.
Shared module-level state instances must be stateless - assigning an attribute to one leaks it into every document using that state.

variants.name: pytransitions Machine attached to a model
variants.implementation_notes: The transitions library attaches a table-driven machine to an existing object: states and transitions are declared as data, the Machine injects trigger methods (doc.publish()) and a state attribute on the model, and callbacks (on_enter_*, before_*, after_*) plus conditions run around every transition. Guards, queued and nested transitions, thread safety options and diagram export come from the library, and the model can even be a dict or a Machine subclass. Choose it when the state graph itself is the artifact to inspect or mutate at runtime; keep hand-written state objects when behaviour, not the graph, is the hard part.
variants.code_sketch:
from transitions import Machine

class Document:
    pass

doc = Document()
machine = Machine(model=doc, states=["draft", "published"], initial="draft")
machine.add_transition("publish", "draft", "published")
doc.publish()
assert doc.state == "published"
pitfalls: The library writes a state attribute and trigger methods onto the model; name clashes are resolved with model_attribute or trigger prefixes.
Callback names are conventions (on_enter_<state>), so typos fail silently unless tests pin the behaviour.
Models equipped with a machine may not pickle or copy naively across library versions; check the serialization notes before persisting them.
